cards.claim: When the second moment decay half-life is held fixed in terms of tokens (not the decay rate β₂), small batch sizes down to batch size 1 train stably and achieve comparable loss to large batch sizes.
cards.conditions: 30M parameter transformer decoder-only model, 600M tokens FineWeb-Edu, context length 512, rotary embeddings, QK-norm, RMSNorm. Batch sizes 1-4096. Adam, SGD, Adafactor, Muon optimizers.
cards.effect: All optimizers achieve similar validation loss at small batch sizes; loss gap between optimizers widens as batch size increases.
cards.evidence: Dense grid search over learning rate, β₁, β₂ jointly tuned for each batch size, reporting lowest validation loss achieved.
cards.quote: if instead of holding fixed, we hold the half-life of fixed (measured in number of tokens), stable training is possible all the way down to batch size one

cards.claim: Vanilla SGD without momentum or weight decay becomes competitive for language model training when batch sizes are small, despite storing no optimizer state.
cards.conditions: 30M parameter transformer, 600M tokens FineWeb-Edu. Batch sizes 1-4096. SGD tuned with learning rate scaling.
cards.effect: SGD achieves comparable validation loss to Adam, Adafactor, and Muon at small batch sizes.
cards.evidence: Grid search with dense hyperparameter tuning; Figure 1(a) showing SGD loss across batch sizes.
cards.quote: we find that even vanilla stochastic gradient descent (SGD), with no momentum or weight decay, becomes competitive for training language models, in contrast to findings from recent work

cards.claim: Small batch sizes exhibit significantly greater robustness to hyperparameter misspecification (learning rate, β₁, β₂) than large batch sizes.
cards.conditions: 30M parameter transformer on FineWeb-Edu (600M tokens). Adam optimizer. Batch sizes 1-4096. Ablation sweeping each hyperparameter while holding others at optimum.
cards.effect: Batch size 1 achieves nearly optimal loss across entire range of learning rates and decay rates tested; batch size 4096 loss increases sharply with hyperparameter variation.
cards.evidence: Loss sensitivity ablation plots (Figure 3) showing scaled hyperparameter values vs. loss for each batch size.
cards.quote: batch size one achieves a nearly optimal loss for the entire range of learning rates, β₁, and τ_β₂ hyperparameters that we consider in our search, whereas the loss for larger batches increases sharply as we vary the hyperparameter values

cards.claim: Learning rate does not scale with the commonly recommended √batch_size rule; empirically it scales much more slowly.
cards.conditions: 30M parameter transformer on FineWeb-Edu. Batch sizes 1-1024. Adam optimizer. Grid search over learning rates at each batch size.
cards.effect: Scaling batch size 1 to 1024 requires ~3× learning rate increase, not 32× as √ rule predicts.
cards.evidence: Grid search validation loss results (Figure 4, left) plotting learning rate sensitivity across batch sizes.
cards.quote: as we scale the batch size from 1 to 1024, the square root rule would indicate that the corresponding learning rate should be scaled by a factor of 32, whereas we find that a factor of only about 3 empirically works better

cards.claim: The default β₁=0.9 (first moment decay) works well across batch sizes without re-tuning, but β₂ (second moment decay) must be adjusted for small batch sizes.
cards.conditions: 30M parameter transformer on FineWeb-Edu. Batch sizes tested 1-1024. Adam optimizer. Grid search over β₁, β₂, learning rate.
cards.effect: Fixed β₁=0.9 achieves good performance across batch sizes; fixed β₂ causes suboptimal performance at small batches; holding β₂ half-life constant avoids re-tuning.
cards.evidence: Grid search validation loss curves (Figure 4) showing loss vs. β₁, β₂, and τ_β₂ across batch sizes.
cards.quote: we also validate that the default value of the first moment decay used by practitioners for language model training does indeed achieve good performance across batch sizes. In contrast, keeping β₂ fixed to its default value...does not scale effectively to smaller batches

cards.claim: Momentum becomes less necessary for small batch sizes because small step sizes with small learning rates do not cause overshooting and oscillations.
cards.conditions: Small batch sizes paired with small learning rates.
cards.effect: Vanilla SGD without momentum performs competitively; momentum not needed for damping.
cards.evidence: Theoretical analysis with toy example in Appendix B; empirical results showing SGD competitive at small batches.
cards.quote: when the optimizer takes small steps, as is the case in small batch training paired with a small learning rate, parameter updates do not overshoot the minimum across short axes, so there are no oscillations to damp

cards.claim: Large batch sizes require more sophisticated optimizers because they require large learning rates that make predictions about the loss surface farther from the current parameter vector.
cards.conditions: Batch size range 1-4096. Multiple optimizers (SGD, Adam, Adafactor, Muon).
cards.effect: Gap between optimizer performance widens with increasing batch size; vanilla SGD lags at large batches but competes at small batches.
cards.evidence: Grid search results across multiple optimizers; Figure 1(a).
cards.quote: When we train with a higher learning rate and take larger steps, for example in large batch training, our optimizer must make predictions about the loss function farther away from the current parameter vector. We hypothesize that taking larger steps leads to a harder prediction problem and that this harder prediction problem requires a more sophisticated or better-tuned optimizer

cards.claim: Fixing the second moment half-life τ_β₂ in tokens (rather than fixing β₂) provides a simple and effective scaling rule across batch sizes with the relationship: τ_β₂(bs') = τ_β₂(bs) × (bs'/bs).
cards.conditions: Adam optimizer across varying batch sizes. 30M parameter transformer on FineWeb-Edu.
cards.effect: Enables good performance when scaling batch size without re-tuning β₂.
cards.evidence: Grid search validation loss (Figure 4) showing that fixed τ_β₂ outperforms fixed β₂ across batch sizes.
cards.quote: keeping β₂ fixed to its optimal value as we scale up or down the batch size provides good performance without re-tuning this hyperparameter at new batch sizes

cards.claim: When Adam hyperparameters are properly tuned (particularly β₂ scaling), small batch sizes can achieve equal or better per-FLOP performance than larger batch sizes.
cards.conditions: 30M and larger models, FineWeb-Edu and C4 datasets, batch sizes 1-4096, Adam optimizer with proper hyperparameter scaling.
cards.effect: Small batch sizes achieve comparable or better validation loss for same FLOP budget.
cards.evidence: Grid search results and reproduction of Xiao [16] experiments with corrected hyperparameter tuning (Figure 5).
cards.quote: we find that small batch sizes (1) train stably, (2) are consistently more robust to hyperparameter choices, (3) achieve equal or better per-FLOP performance than larger batch sizes
